summary: Decide whether t is a rearrangement of the letters of s.
mainInsight: Two strings are anagrams iff every character appears the same number of times in both. Counting characters (array of 26 or a hash map) gets this in one pass instead of sorting.

approaches.name: Two hash maps / Counter
strengths: Works for any alphabet incl. Unicode
approaches.interviewRelevance: The answer to the Unicode follow-up.

approaches.name: Single 26-slot count array
approaches.summary: Increment for s[i], decrement for t[i]; all slots must end at 0.
approaches.interviewRelevance: The expected answer for lowercase letters.

personalSolution.notes: Optimal for lowercase letters. Remember the Counter/hash-map version for the Unicode follow-up.

promptVariants: Which technique solves this problem, and what in the statement or constraints points to it?
Name the technique you would use here and the clue in the problem that tells you.
What approach fits this problem, and which part of the statement gives it away?
cards.answer: Compare letter frequencies (a 26-slot count array or a counter). Clue: Anagrams are exactly the strings with identical letter counts, and the alphabet is only the lowercase letters, so compare counts.
keyPoints: Anagrams are exactly the strings with identical letter counts, and the alphabet is only the lowercase letters, so compare counts.
cards.explanation: Equal multisets of letters is the definition of an anagram, and counting 26 letters checks it in one pass.

rubric.technique: Compare letter frequencies (a 26-slot count array or a counter)
rubric.clue: Anagrams are exactly the strings with identical letter counts, and the alphabet is only the lowercase letters, so compare counts.

promptVariants: What approach checks an anagram in O(n)?
Which technique fits 'same multiset of characters'?

incorrectOptionExplanations.Two pointers from both ends: That checks palindromes, not multiset equality.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Sliding window: No contiguous window constraint (that is the 'find anagrams in a string' variant).

promptVariants: Why does one count array with +1/-1 work?
Explain how the single-array increment/decrement trick proves an anagram.
cards.answer: Each position adds 1 for s's letter and subtracts 1 for t's letter. If the multisets are equal every count cancels to 0; any non-zero slot means some letter appears more in one string. The length check guarantees no leftover letters.
cards.explanation: It merges two count tables into one.

promptVariants: Time complexity of the count-array solution: ___
Valid Anagram with counting is ___ time.
cards.explanation: One pass over the strings plus a 26-step check.

promptVariants: Why is the space O(1) for lowercase letters but not in general?
What changes if the strings can contain Unicode?
cards.answer: The array has a fixed 26 slots independent of n, so O(1). For Unicode the alphabet is large/unbounded, so use a hash map (O(k) distinct characters) instead of a fixed array.

promptVariants: Why is `len(s) != len(t) -> False` worth checking first?
What does the early length check buy you?
options: Different lengths can never be anagrams; it saves work and errors
It makes the whole solution run in O(1) time and O(1) space
It is only required for the correctness of the count array
It handles Unicode strings that the counting loop would miss
cards.answer: Different lengths can never be anagrams; it saves work and errors
cards.explanation: The paired loop indexes t[i] for every i in s, so unequal lengths would break it.

incorrectOptionExplanations.It is only required for the correctness: It is also an early exit; it is mainly required for the paired loop.

promptVariants: Why does your final loop only need to check `arr[i] != 0`, and what would a positive/negative value indicate?
In the count-array solution, what do positive and negative leftovers mean and why is checking for non-zero enough?
cards.answer: Since lengths are equal, the counts sum to 0, so any non-zero entry implies some other entry is non-zero with the opposite sign. A positive value means s has more of that letter; negative means t has more. Any non-zero => not an anagram.
keyPoints: Positive: s has more; negative: t has more
cards.explanation: Equal lengths guarantee a deficit somewhere if there is a surplus.

promptVariants: How would you solve it for Unicode input, and what is the cost?
What changes in Valid Anagram if the inputs may contain arbitrary Unicode characters?
cards.answer: Use collections.Counter (hash maps) for s and t and compare, or increment/decrement a single dict and check all zero. O(n) time, O(k) space for k distinct characters.
keyPoints: Hash map instead of fixed array
